_comment: WHAT KIND OF PICTURE this is. The fifth axis, added 2026-09-13, after the household asked
for pictures that are not all the same kind of picture: 'a Where's Waldo style... a
photorealistic image but of an unrealistic thing... riding unicorns or Pegasus... wearing a
Spiderman suit and swinging from a building.' Setting says WHERE, style says HOW IT IS
DRAWN, camera says WHERE YOU STAND, activities say WHAT THEY DO. None of those can say
'the children are giants' or 'this is a cutaway of a house' — that is a different premise
for the whole picture, and it changes several of the other axes at once.
A premise is applied by gen-scene.py `--premise <id>` and does up to five things: adds a
PREMISE section right after SCENE; replaces the LAYOUT section; replaces the crowd
sentence; replaces the activity pool; restricts the style families it may be drawn in;
and `solo_only` keeps the shared activities out (a seek-and-find with two children carrying
one basket is a huddle, and a cutaway must never put two in one room — measured 2026-09-13).
`plain` does none of them and is what every scene before this file was. Anything a
premise does not override is inherited, so a premise is a small file and the identity
contract (count, height order, hair — THE THREE CHILDREN) is never touched by one.
THE MECHANIC SETS THE LIMITS, not taste. Three children find themselves in this picture
and tap themselves, so every premise has to keep: (1) each child at least 1.5 inches tall
on the glass — scene-regions.py refuses smaller, which is why a true Waldo-grade picture
with the children a tenth of the frame is not in this file and will not be; (2) hair
visible — no mask, no helmet, no hood, which is why the superhero has a cape and no mask
and the astronaut carries the helmet; (3) faces to the viewer; (4) clear ground between
the three — anything that seats them together (three on one dragon) fights the tap gutter;
(5) whatever a child rides or drives, she is ON it in the open, never inside a cab or
behind glass — a child inside a monster truck is a windscreen, not a tap target.
NO NAMED CHARACTERS OR BRANDS, same reasoning as scene-settings.json's fantasy settings:
gpt-image-2 refused named characters on 92% of attempts and nano-banana-2 on 42% in an
August 2026 study, so a named suit is a coin-flip on one model and a refusal on the other;
and the costume would be competing with the child for the viewer's attention on a screen
whose one job is that she finds herself. 'A red-and-blue superhero suit with a cape' is
the whole idea without the trademark.
NOTHING HOUSEHOLD-SPECIFIC GOES IN HERE. Sent verbatim to a hosted model; prompt_guard reads
the assembled prompt and will refuse anyway.

premises.label: An ordinary scene
premises.wall: What every picture before 2026-09-13 was. The default when no premise is given, and the one the weekly run uses until the household chooses otherwise.

premises.label: Seek-and-find crowd
premises.wall: The Wimmelbuch / seek-and-find treatment. REWRITTEN 2026-09-24 after the first attempt put a second braided figure in the crowd and the finder tapped her instead of the eldest. The old rule was NEGATIVE — 'no other child shares hair colour and length with one of ours' — which asks a model to hold three descriptions in mind while drawing forty figures and check each one against all three. It does not, and a near-miss is invisible until a verifier taps the wrong girl. The household's fix is positive and structural: EVERY other figure's head is covered. Hair then belongs to the three children by construction rather than by avoidance, there is nothing to compare and nothing to get wrong, and the hats are a gift to the picture — forty different heads in forty different coverings is exactly the visual density this premise wants. It also hands the finder an unambiguous search with no change to the finder: the only bare heads in the frame are the three it is looking for. FLAT SCALE, added the same day: this premise and the find-difficulty bands are in direct contradiction — the bands put one child near the front and one well back, and the whole point of a busy-picture is that NOBODY is nearer or larger than anybody else. The premise wins, because in a seek-and-find everyone is equally hidden and that IS the difficulty. `flat_scale` drops the placement clause from the prompt and drops the per-child height floors in the finder back to the single `MIN_CHILD_HEIGHT_IN`, which is the right floor when every figure is drawn the same size. Without the second half the youngest is refused for being small in a picture where small is the instruction — measured 2026-09-24, he came out 1.50in against his own 1.80in floor.
premises.brief:
This is a seek-and-find picture in the tradition of the big wordless busy-picture books: the whole place teems with dozens of small figures, all drawn at ONE consistent scale from a raised viewpoint, and the three children are hidden in plain sight among everyone else. There is no foreground group: nobody is nearer the camera or larger than anybody else.

EVERY CORNER IS DOING SOMETHING. Fill it with small complete stories a child can find and laugh at — someone chasing a hat down the street, a dog running off with a sausage, a ladder wobbling with a painter on it, a cat watching a fishmonger, someone asleep in a window box, a juggler dropping everything, a queue where one person is clearly cheating, a spilled basket of apples rolling downhill with three people after them. Nothing violent and nobody hurt: the joke is always that a small thing has gone charmingly wrong.
premises.layout: The three children are small — each is about a fifth of the picture's height, no taller than the grown-ups beside them, and they stand in the middle of the crowd, not in front of it. They are far apart from one another: one on the left, one in the middle and one on the right, each doing her own thing with clear ground on every side and nothing in front of her. Each child's face is towards the viewer (front on, three-quarter or profile) with head and body turned the same way.
premises.crowd:
The place is packed edge to edge with life, forty or more figures at the same scale as the three children: {crowd}.

EVERY SINGLE PERSON IN THE CROWD HAS THEIR HEAD COVERED — every adult and every other child, without exception. Give them all different coverings and make them part of the fun: flat caps, sun hats, woolly hats, hoods up, bike helmets, hard hats, chef's hats, headscarves, bonnets, party hats, a bucket, a newspaper folded into a hat. Not one of them shows their hair.
premises.nearest: THE THREE CHILDREN ARE THE ONLY BARE HEADS IN THE WHOLE PICTURE. Their hair is uncovered and plainly visible — no hat, no hood, no helmet, nothing over it — and every other figure in the frame, adult or child, has theirs covered. That difference is the entire game: a child finds herself by looking for the only hair of her colour in the scene.

premises.label: A cutaway house
premises.wall: A dollhouse cross-section: the front wall gone, every room a bright little stage, one child per room. The best fit of all of these for the tap mechanic — a room is a natural cell with walls for gutters — and a genre the children already know from their picture books. The building comes from this premise, not from the week's setting; the setting stays around and behind it as the view out of the windows and the garden in front.
premises.brief: This is a cutaway picture: {building}, seen straight on with its whole front wall removed, so every room inside is visible at once like a dollhouse — each room a bright, fully furnished little stage with its own things going on, stacked and side by side, with stairs and doorways joining them. The building stands in the middle of the picture and the place described above is what surrounds it and shows through its windows.
premises.layout: {The_children} are in {count} DIFFERENT rooms, each child alone in her room and each room clearly separated from the next by a wall or a floor. Each child is at least a quarter of the picture's height tall and faces the viewer (front on, three-quarter or profile) with head and body turned the same way.
premises.crowd: The other rooms, the stairs, the roof and the garden are full of life: {crowd}.
buildings: a tall, narrow, slightly crooked house of five or six rooms with an attic and a cellar
a lighthouse with a spiral stair and round rooms stacked to the lamp at the top
a treehouse of many platforms and rope bridges built through one enormous tree
an old sailing ship, hull and decks opened up, with cabins, a galley and a crow's nest
a castle tower with a great hall, a kitchen, a library and a dungeon at the bottom
a hollow giant tree fitted out with rooms, ladders and round windows
a big red barn with a hayloft, stalls and a workshop

premises.label: Three giants
premises.wall: The three children are giants striding through a tiny town — taller than the houses, careful where they step. Huge tap targets, hair impossible to hide, and the crowd becomes a miniature world at their feet. Works in any family, and it is the cheapest premise for the finder: three big figures and nothing in front of them.
premises.brief: {The_children} are GIANTS. They are taller than the houses and the trees, and they move carefully through a tiny version of the place described above, whose people, animals and vehicles come up to their ankles and look up at them in delight.
premises.layout: Each of the {count} fills most of the picture's height, standing on the ground among the tiny buildings, spread across the picture with clear sky between one and the next — never overlapping and never in a huddle. Each child's face is towards the viewer (front on, three-quarter or profile) with head and body turned the same way.
premises.crowd: At their feet the tiny place is busy and full of life: {crowd}; everything and everyone in it small enough to stand in a child's palm.
premises.nearest: They are the only {count} children at giant scale; any tiny children in the town below are the size of toys.

premises.label: Mouse-sized
premises.wall: The opposite of giants: the children are the size of mice, so a daisy is a tree, a beetle is a pony and a puddle is a lake. The weekly setting is kept but seen from ankle height, which quietly gives every setting a second life. The finder's floor still applies — they are small IN THE STORY, not in the frame.
premises.brief: {The_children} are TINY — no bigger than mice — and the place described above is seen from their height: grass blades tower like trees, a fallen leaf is a boat, a pebble is a boulder, an ordinary beetle is the size of a pony, and everyday things loom enormous and wonderful around them.
premises.layout: Although tiny in the story, {the_children} are LARGE in the picture — each at least a quarter of the picture's height — because the picture is taken from down at their own scale. They are spread across the scene with clear ground between them, never a huddle. Each child's face is towards the viewer (front on, three-quarter or profile) with head and body turned the same way.
premises.crowd: Around them, at their own tiny scale, the ground is busy: ants carrying crumbs, a ladybird, a snail, a grasshopper, a dandelion clock, spilled seeds, a dropped button, a lost marble; and far above and out of focus, the ordinary world of {crowd}.

activities.do: riding a friendly beetle like a pony
riding on the back of a bumblebee just above the flowers
sailing a leaf boat across a puddle with a twig for a mast
climbing a dandelion stalk to blow its seeds
climbing a mushroom to sit on its cap
sliding down a long blade of grass
bouncing on a mushroom cap like a trampoline
rolling a marble much bigger than a football
sheltering under a mushroom from a single enormous raindrop
swinging on a spider's thread like a rope swing
sharing a strawberry the size of a house with a mouse

premises.label: A toy-box world
premises.wall: Everything in the place is a toy at the children's own size — block houses they can duck into, wooden cone trees as tall as they are, a train set for a road — and they are the only soft, living figures in it. NOT giants: the toys are child-scale and the children walk through them, where `giants` puts a tiny town at their ankles. Written 2026-10-29, untested. The identity trick is the busy-town one made structural: every other person is a wooden peg doll with a smooth painted bead for a head, so hair belongs to the children by construction. Strongest in the `render` family (soft-3d, claymation), where glossy paint and wood grain are free. Watch for: a peg doll drawn with painted-on hair in a child's colour (the finder's look-alike check is the backstop), and the dog rendered as a plush toy — he is named after the crowd sentence and should still be himself.
premises.brief: This is a picture of a TOY-BOX WORLD: the place described above has been built entirely out of toys and stands on a wooden playroom floor. The trees are painted wooden cones and bottle-brush pines, the houses are stacked building blocks with hinged roofs and painted-on windows, the hills are folded green felt, the river is a strip of shiny blue ribbon, the road is a wooden train track with a clockwork engine puffing round it, and the sky is the warm, plain wall of the playroom. Everything has the smooth, glossy, slightly chunky look of a well-loved toy: visible wood grain, thick paint, a wind-up key in the side of a tin car, stitches on a plush animal. The toys are built at the children's own size — a block house they could duck into, a wooden tree as tall as they are, a toy car they could sit on — and {the_children} are the only soft, living people in it, as if they had climbed into the toy box to play.
premises.layout: {The_children} are spread across the toy world with clear floor between them, each at least a quarter of the picture's height, each standing upright or sitting up straight on the playroom floor among the toys at their own size, never crouching or kneeling, never on top of one another and never in a huddle. Each child's face is towards the viewer (front on, three-quarter or profile) with head and body turned the same way.
premises.crowd: The toy world is crowded with toy versions of the place: {crowd} — every one of them made as a toy. EVERY PERSON among them is a wooden peg doll with a smooth, round, painted bead for a head and no hair at all: two painted dots for eyes, a painted smile, a painted coat. Peg dolls sit in toy carts, stand at toy stalls and lean against blocks everywhere, and the animals are plush animals with stitched seams or carved wooden ones on little wheels.
premises.nearest: {The_children} are the only children in the picture, and the only figures with hair, soft faces and cloth clothes; every other person in it is a smooth-headed wooden peg doll.
premises.rules: Every block is one plain painted colour on every face, every toy box is bare varnished wood, and every tin toy is painted in plain stripes and spots.

activities.do: stacking painted wooden blocks into a tower taller than themselves
building a bridge of wooden planks over the ribbon river
riding a wooden rocking horse painted with stars
sitting on a big wind-up tin car and turning its key
pushing a toy train along the wooden track behind its puffing engine
rolling a huge wooden ball down a felt hill
setting a striped top as tall as their waist spinning with one hand
winding up a tin robot and watching it walk
lifting the hinged roof off a block house to look inside
lining up wooden ducks on wheels in a long row
pulling a wooden duck on a string across the floor
tapping a wooden xylophone with a mallet

premises.label: A land made of food
premises.wall: The place rebuilt out of things to eat — loaf hills, broccoli trees, a honey river, gingerbread houses — at the children's size, so a biscuit is a stepping stone and a strawberry comes up to a knee. The thing a three-year-old points at first. Written 2026-10-29, untested. Same structural identity trick as toy-world: every other person is a gingerbread figure with a smooth biscuit head, so no hair in the frame but the children's. Textures are the whole picture (crust, glossy icing, sugar sparkle), which suits every family and especially `render`. Watch for: wrappers and packets — they carry print, so the brief names only unwrapped food; and a model reading 'at the children's size' as 'the children are tiny', which would make it a `tiny` variant. The layout says they stand on the food ground at ordinary size.
premises.brief: This is a picture of a LAND MADE OF FOOD: the place described above is built entirely out of things to eat. The hills are crusty loaves of bread, the trees are stalks of broccoli and sticks of pink candyfloss, the rocks are muffins and cupcakes, the path is a row of round biscuits, the river is slow golden honey, the ponds are bowls of wobbling jelly, the houses have gingerbread walls, white icing roofs and clear sugar-pane windows, and the fences are breadsticks. It is all built at the children's own scale: a loaf is a hill they can climb, a biscuit is a stepping stone, a strawberry comes up to a child's knee. The textures are the point — crumbly crust, glossy icing, the dimples on a strawberry, sugar sparkling on a sponge — in warm, bright, delicious colours.
premises.layout: {The_children} are drawn just as their portraits show them, with their own hair and their own heights, and they are the only things in the land not made of food. They are their ordinary size, standing on the food ground among the loaves and the biscuits, spread across the scene with clear ground between them and each at least a quarter of the picture's height, never in a huddle. Each child's face is towards the viewer (front on, three-quarter or profile) with head and body turned the same way.
premises.crowd: The land is busy: {crowd} — all of it made of food. EVERY PERSON among them is a gingerbread person with a smooth, round biscuit head, icing eyes and an icing smile, sugar buttons down the front and no hair at all; the animals are marzipan animals and sugar mice.
premises.nearest: {The_children} are the only children in the picture, and the only figures with hair; every other person in it is a smooth-headed gingerbread figure.
premises.rules: Every piece of food is bare, straight from the oven or the bowl: plain crusty bread, plain biscuits, bare boiled sweets and sugar in heaps.

activities.do: climbing a crusty loaf-of-bread hill
climbing a ladder of breadsticks up the side of a cake
sliding down a long curved spoon into a bowl of jelly
sailing a hollowed bread roll across a pond of blue jelly
rolling a giant green pea along a biscuit path
bouncing on a wobbling pond of jelly
picking sugar flowers in a meadow of green icing
knocking on the icing door of a gingerbread house
catching marshmallows that drift down like snow
holding a lollipop twice as tall as themselves
stacking pancakes into a leaning tower
riding a sugar mouse the size of a pony

premises.label: A giant board game
premises.wall: The place has become the board: a path of big flat coloured squares snakes across the ground, a die the size of a shed, a spinner, a ladder and a slide between squares, and the children are the players standing ON the path. Written 2026-10-29, untested. Pins `high-angle` so the path reads as a path. The squares do the finder's work — one child per square with empty squares between, which is the cutaway's rooms laid flat. The other players are wooden pawns with no hair and no faces. Watch for: anything on the board that wants print — the brief says plain single-colour squares, round black dots on the die, coloured wedges on the spinner, and the rules say so again; a board game is the one premise here whose props carry numbers in real life, so this is the risk to look at first.
premises.brief: This is a picture of a GIANT BOARD GAME: the place described above has become the board, and a winding path of big flat coloured squares — red, yellow, blue, green, one after another, each a single plain colour and each big enough for a child to stand on — snakes across the ground from one corner of the picture to the other, over the hills and between the buildings. Scattered about the board at a size to match are the pieces of the game: a wooden die as big as a garden shed with round black dots on its faces, a spinner with coloured wedges and a big pointer, tall painted playing pieces shaped like pawns, a stack of round wooden counters, a little ladder leaning from one square up to a higher one and a curly slide running from a high square down to a low one. {The_children} are the players.
premises.layout: {The_children} are each at a DIFFERENT square of the path, well apart along it with several empty squares between one child and the next — standing on the square itself, all of them on the near half of the board in the lower two-thirds of the picture — each at least a quarter of the picture's height. Each child's face is towards the viewer (front on, three-quarter or profile) with head and body turned the same way.
premises.crowd: Around the board the place carries on at its own size: {crowd}; and the OTHER PLAYERS waiting beside the path are tall wooden pawns and painted playing pieces — smooth and rounded, with no hair and no faces — standing on squares of their own.
premises.nearest: {The_children} are the only children in the picture; every other player on the board is a wooden playing piece.
premises.rules: Every square of the path is one flat plain colour, the die shows only round black dots, and the spinner shows only coloured wedges.

activities.do: pushing over a wooden die as big as a garden shed
rolling a round wooden counter along the path like a hoop
climbing a little ladder from one square up to the next
landing at the foot of a curly slide with both arms up
spinning a giant spinner with both hands
hopping from one coloured square to the next
sitting on a stack of giant round counters
pushing a tall wooden pawn along the path
standing on top of a huge wooden die with arms out wide
leaning on a tall wooden pawn and grinning

premises.label: Leading the parade
premises.wall: The children at the very front of a parade coming towards the viewer through the place, with the band, the dancers, the stilt-walkers and a swan float stretching away behind them. Written 2026-10-29, untested. Pins `close-front`: the parade's leaders are by definition the nearest and largest, which is exactly the finder's rule, and the whole crowd is behind them where it cannot cover anyone. The hair trick is busy-town's: everyone in the parade and the crowd has a plumed hat, a paper crown, a flower wreath or a jester cap, so the only bare heads are the children's. Watch for: a child given a band hat too (the layout says bare heads, HAIR_V2 says it again), and the children drawn shoulder to shoulder in one marching rank — the layout asks for a loose line with clear ground between. No flags: a flag wants an emblem, and an emblem wants lettering. `flat_scale` is set, as in busy-town, because the find-difficulty bands would put a leader "well back, genuinely hidden".
premises.brief: This is a picture of a PARADE, and {the_children} are at the very front of it, leading it towards the viewer through the place described above. Behind them the parade stretches back into the distance: a marching band with big brass horns and drums, dancers in swirling skirts, stilt-walkers, jugglers, a pony pulling a cart heaped with flowers, a float shaped like a huge swan, bunches of balloons on strings, paper streamers and confetti in the air, and a cheering, waving crowd lining both sides. The light is bright and festive, the colours are the colours of balloons and bunting — red, yellow, sky blue, white — and everything in it is in motion.
premises.layout: {The_children} walk at the head of the parade, in a loose line across the front of the picture with clear ground between one and the next — never shoulder to shoulder — each at least a quarter of the picture's height and nearer and larger than anyone behind them, with their hair bare and uncovered. Each child's face is towards the viewer (front on, three-quarter or profile) with head and body turned the same way.
premises.crowd: Marching behind them and cheering from both sides are {crowd}, all part of the parade. EVERY PERSON in the parade and in the crowd is a grown-up, and every one has their head covered as part of the show, each one differently: tall plumed band hats, paper crowns, flower wreaths, jester caps, bonnets, bandanas, feathered hats, pointed party hats. Not one of them shows their hair.
premises.nearest: {The_children} are the only children and the only bare heads in the whole picture: their hair is uncovered and plainly visible, and every other person, in the parade or watching it, has theirs covered. They are the nearest and largest figures in the picture.

activities.do: beating a big drum hung on a strap over one shoulder
blowing a long brass trumpet
banging two shiny cymbals together
twirling a baton high in the air
waving a long rainbow ribbon on a stick in loops
waving to the crowd with both hands
riding on a small flower-covered cart pulled by a pony
scattering handfuls of confetti into the air
holding a big bunch of balloons on strings
walking on short stilts with a big grin
doing a high-stepping march with knees up

premises.label: An underwater day
premises.wall: The place has filled with clear sunlit sea water over the rooftops and everyone carries on with their day on the bottom as if water were air: fish between the branches, a turtle past a window, bubbles off everything. Written 2026-10-29, untested. The fully-clothed rule stands untouched (ordinary clothes, underwater, is the joke), nothing is on any face, and hair drifts but keeps its colour. The one real risk is ORIENTATION: a model's idea of 'underwater' is a horizontal swimmer, and the finder refuses anything not upright. The layout says UPRIGHT, heads up and feet down, twice; the activities keep them on the bottom (riding a turtle, collecting shells, sitting on a clam) and none of them floats up. If the first draw comes back with a child lying flat, that is this premise failing, not the art. Second risk: still water and a mirror surface above would draw the children twice; the brief keeps the surface far overhead and out of frame.
premises.brief: This is an UNDERWATER picture: the place described above has filled up with clear, bright, sunlit sea water, right up over the treetops and the rooftops and far out of the top of the picture, and everyone is carrying on with their day down on the bottom as if the water were air. Shafts of sunlight slant down through the water, shoals of small striped fish drift between the branches, a slow sea turtle paddles past a window, seaweed sways where the grass was, a crab sits on a doorstep, an octopus reads in a chair, and strings of silver bubbles rise from everything. The colours are the blue-green of shallow sea with sunlight rippling across the ground. Everyone is in their ordinary clothes and breathes the water as easily as air, with nothing on any face, and hair lifts and drifts gently in the water while staying exactly its own colour and plainly visible.
premises.layout: {The_children} are UPRIGHT on the bottom — heads up, feet down, standing or stepping along the ground as if on dry land, never lying flat and never tilted — spread across the scene with clear water between them, each at least a quarter of the picture's height, their whole body in clear water from head to feet with nothing in front of it. Each child's face is towards the viewer (front on, three-quarter or profile) with head and body turned the same way. Their hair drifts a little in the water but stays its own colour and plainly visible.
premises.crowd: Around them, carrying on underwater as if nothing were different: {crowd}; and among them, at their ordinary size, an octopus, a sea turtle, a shoal of small striped fish, a seahorse, a crab and a pink anemone.
premises.rules: Nothing in the picture is lying flat or floating sideways: every person is upright with their head above their feet.

activities.do: walking beside a slow sea turtle with a hand on its shell
holding the reins of a big friendly seahorse bobbing beside them
blowing a long stream of silver bubbles
bouncing along the bottom in big slow moon-steps
waving at a curious octopus
collecting shells into a little bucket
scattering crumbs for a shoal of striped fish
standing beside an open chest full of pearls holding up a string of them
standing beside a giant open clam shell holding up a pearl
holding an open umbrella against a drift of rising bubbles

premises.label: The stars come down
premises.wall: A night picture in which the animals of the night sky — a bear, a swan, a lion, a horse, a hare — have climbed down out of the sky to play in the place, each made of bright points of light joined by thin glowing lines, see-through, and glowing enough to light the whole scene like a full moon. Written 2026-10-29, untested. The point of the glow clause is the 225-nit panel: hair colour is the identity and a dark picture loses it, so the creatures are the light source and the children are explicitly solid and fully coloured, never see-through. Sky stays plain (a few small stars) because RULES_V2 owns the top of the picture — the creatures are DOWN, which is the whole premise. Watch for: a child drawn in the same line-and-point style as the creatures (the layout forbids it), and darkness swallowing a brunette. Pairs naturally with lantern-night and dreamlike; works in render too.
premises.brief: This is a NIGHT picture in which the STAR CREATURES HAVE COME DOWN TO PLAY. The great animals of the night sky — a bear, a swan, a lion, a horse, a hare, a deer, a dolphin — have climbed down out of the sky into the place described above, and each one is made of bright points of starlight joined by thin glowing lines, see-through, with the dark place showing faintly through its body. They stand and play among the trees and houses at the size of living animals, and they glow so brightly that the whole scene is lit as if by a full moon: every face, every head of hair and every colour is clear and bright in their blue-white light. Above, the sky is deep dark blue with only a few small stars left in it, empty where the creatures climbed down.
premises.layout: {The_children} stand on the ground among the star creatures, each lit bright by them, spread across the scene with clear ground between them and each at least a quarter of the picture's height. They are solid and fully coloured, drawn exactly like any child in daylight and never see-through or made of lines; only the star creatures glow. Each child's face is towards the viewer (front on, three-quarter or profile) with head and body turned the same way.
premises.crowd: The place at night is quiet but not empty: {crowd}, all of it bathed in the soft blue-white light of the star creatures.

activities.do: stroking the glowing nose of a star bear
walking beside a star bear with one hand on its shoulder
riding a star horse made of joined points of light
dancing hand in paw with a star hare in a ring of light
catching a small falling star in cupped hands
tossing a glowing ball to a star lion
holding a glowing star up high like a lantern
tracing the glowing lines of a star swan with one finger
feeding a star deer a handful of glowing berries

premises.label: Painting the picture in
premises.wall: The children are painting the picture themselves and are only part-way through: the left and middle are the place in full colour, and towards the right the paint runs out into a wash, then pencil outlines, then bare white paper. Each child holds a brush, roller or crayon far bigger than an ordinary one. Written 2026-10-29, untested. The seven-year-old's premise: it is a picture ABOUT making pictures. Finder risk is contrast — a child standing in the unpainted part is pale lines on white — so the layout puts every child in the finished part and says they are always completely painted from head to toe. Illustration and anime only: 'half painted' has no honest meaning for a 3D render. Watch for: the model painting the top of the picture (sky) rather than the ground; and paint on faces, which FACE_COVER would refuse in a written line and the brief avoids by keeping the paint on brushes, trees and hands.

premises.label: Every season at once
premises.wall: The place drawn in every season at once: side-by-side slices across the width — snow, blossom, full summer, red and gold leaves — with the same trees and path running straight through all of them, and each child in a DIFFERENT season. Written 2026-10-29, untested. The slices are cells for the finder, the way the cutaway's rooms are. The trick that makes it work with the activity dealer: the activity pool's `family` IS the season, so 'at most one per family' deals each child a different season for free, and the layout says a child stands in the season their activity belongs to. Cast is 2 to 4 because there are four seasons. Watch for: the week's weather line (in SCENE) arguing with three of the four slices — the brief says every season on purpose; and seams drawn as literal lines or posts. `--no-context` is a reasonable pairing. Clothes change per slice, which the identity contract allows (clothes were always meant to vary) — hair stays bare in every one.
premises.brief: This is a picture of the place described above in EVERY SEASON AT ONCE. The picture is divided across its width into side-by-side slices, each one the same place in a different season, joined edge to edge: deep snow, bare branches and a low pale sun in one; blossom, fresh green and puddles in the next; full summer leaves, long grass and bright hot sunshine in another; red and gold falling leaves and a soft golden light in the last. The same trees, the same path and the same buildings run straight on through all of them, changing their coats as they cross from one season into the next, and the change is sudden and clean, like a line drawn straight down the picture. {The_children} are each in a DIFFERENT season.
premises.layout: {The_children} each stand in a DIFFERENT season — the one that what they are doing belongs to — one child per slice, well apart across the picture, each of them in the picture exactly once; a season with none of them in it holds only the place itself and a few small strangers far off, each at least a quarter of the picture's height and dressed for the season around them: a warm coat, mittens and earmuffs in the snow, a raincoat and boots in spring, a t-shirt and shorts in summer, a jumper in autumn, with hair bare and plainly visible in every one. Each child's face is towards the viewer (front on, three-quarter or profile) with head and body turned the same way.
premises.crowd: Each season's slice has its own life: {crowd}, shared out across the seasons and doing what suits each one — sledging where it snows, splashing where it rains, picnicking in the sunshine, kicking through leaves in the autumn.

premises.label: A day with the dinosaurs
premises.wall: The place exactly as it should be, and every other PERSON in it is a gentle, round-bellied dinosaur going about that person's business — a long-necked one with a shopping basket, a three-horned one pushing a pram, a small feathered one on a bicycle. Written 2026-10-29, untested. The crowd-swap family of premise: setting untouched, identity made structural because a dinosaur has no hair, and the children are the only people in the picture at all. The brief says PERSON, not creature, so the dog clause that follows the crowd sentence still describes him and not a dinosaur. Watch for: a house-high dinosaur standing in front of a child (the layout says around and behind, never in front), and a dinosaur drawn with teeth and a roar — kind eyes and gentle smiles are named instead. Describe, never name: no species names, only shapes.
premises.brief: This is a picture in which EVERY OTHER PERSON IS A FRIENDLY DINOSAUR. The place described above is exactly as it should be, and all the people who would normally be in it are gentle, round-bellied, cheerful dinosaurs going about the very same business on two legs or four: a long-necked one with a shopping basket, a three-horned one pushing a pram, a small feathered one on a bicycle, a big spiky-backed one carrying a ladder, a tiny crested one holding a balloon — in soft greens, oranges, blues and spotted yellows, with kind eyes and gentle smiles. Some are as tall as a house and some are knee-high, and all of them are perfectly at home.
premises.layout: {The_children} are spread across the scene with clear ground between them, each at least a quarter of the picture's height, with the dinosaurs around and behind them and never in front of a child. A dinosaur a child is with stands BESIDE that child, an arm's length away, never behind or over them, so the child's whole body and face stand clear of it. Each child's face is towards the viewer (front on, three-quarter or profile) with head and body turned the same way.
premises.crowd: The place is as busy as ever: {crowd} — and every PERSON among them is one of the dinosaurs, in every size from knee-high to house-high, doing exactly what that person would be doing.
premises.nearest: {The_children} are the only children in the picture — the only people at all; everyone else is a dinosaur.
premises.rules: Every dinosaur is dressed only in its own bare scaly skin, in its own colours.
